source1: Klaus Schippmann, 'Arsacids ii. The Arsacid Dynasty', Encyclopaedia Iranica II/5, 1986 - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/arsacids-ii
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ardashir I' (Parthian kingship still in place in 224) - https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ardashir-I
notes: No break c.40 CE: Arsacid succession continued (Artabanus II, Vardanes I, Gotarzes II); period split only. Q4: Roman-backed Tiridates 35-37, Seleucia revolt 36-42, Vardanes-Gotarzes rivalry. Arsacid authority actually ended 224 (see F231).

successor: Cahokia - Late Woodland III (continuing local Late Woodland communities)
source1: J. Grant Stauffer et al., 'Reimagining the Development of Downtown Cahokia Using Remote Sensing Visualizations from the Western Edge of the Grand Plaza', Land 12(2):342, MDPI 2023 - https://www.mdpi.com/2073-445X/12/2/342
notes: Dispersed Late Woodland villagers, no central authority. Stauffer et al. report landscape management from c.450 CE and gradual village aggregation 650-850; nothing indicates a break at 600. Inference only; no second source could be opened.

successor: Ghuzz (Oghuz) chiefs and Turkish amirs in Khurasan; later Khwarazmshahs
source1: Deborah G. Tor, 'Sanjar, Ahmad b. Malekshah', Encyclopaedia Iranica, 2000 (updated 2012) - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/sanjar
notes: Core = Merv, Sanjar's capital. Subject Ghuzz Turkmen defeated and held Sanjar 1153-56; he died at Merv 1157; Khurasan fragmented among Ghuzz and amirs until Khwarazmian absorption. Qatwan defeat 1141. Hamadan Seljuks lasted to 1194; Il-Khanate successor wrong.

source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'White Lotus Rebellion' (1796-1804) - https://www.britannica.com/event/White-Lotus-Rebellion ; also Britannica, 'Qianlong' (reign 1735-1796) - https://www.britannica.com/biography/Qianlong
notes: 1796 = end of Qianlong's reign and accession of Jiaqing; the Qing state and Beijing court continued to 1911/12, so this is a period split. Q4: large White Lotus Rebellion (1796-1804) broke out at the end date.

source2: C. E. Bosworth, 'Kalaf b. Ahmad', Encyclopaedia Iranica - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/kalaf-b-ahmad ; also Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Saffarid dynasty' - https://www.britannica.com/topic/Saffarid-dynasty
notes: Mahmud of Ghazna invaded Sistan 393/1002-3, besieged and deposed Khalaf b. Ahmad, and annexed Sistan as a Ghaznavid province. Prior strife: Khalaf's war with Hosayn b. Taher (to 983) and feud with son Taher (d.1002).

source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ethiopia: The Zagwe and Solomonic dynasties' - https://www.britannica.com/place/Ethiopia/The-Zagwe-and-Solomonic-dynasties
notes: Ifat tributary to Ethiopia after Amda Seyon's 1328 victory, then repeatedly revolted; Ethiopia destroyed and annexed it after defeating Sa'd ad-Din II (Britannica: 1415; other Britannica text: 1445). Database 1375 likely marks Walashma shift toward Harar/Adal.

source2: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Dept. of Asian Art, 'Yayoi Culture (ca. 300 B.C.-300 A.D.)', Heilbrunn Timeline, 2002 - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/yayo/hd_yayo.htm
notes: Archaeological phase: Kinai Yayoi had clan-based chiefly polities but no securely located central authority (Yamatai disputed). Kofun mound culture followed without documented conquest or population replacement. Sources weak; continuity only indirectly supported.

successor: Competing Zapotec petty polities of the Valley of Oaxaca (Monte Alban V)
source1: Ronald K. Faulseit, 'State Collapse and Household Resilience in the Oaxaca Valley of Mexico', Latin American Antiquity 23(4):401-425, 2012 - https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/latin-american-antiquity/article/abs/state-collapse-and-household-resilience-in-the-oaxaca-valley-of-mexico/9C869A1400C36983438C55932C240443
notes: Late Classic political fragmentation: Monte Alban lost political pre-eminence c.700-850 as subordinate centres became autonomous competing polities; capital later largely abandoned; no conquest documented. Database 900 is phase end; collapse earlier.
